course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Contextualizing Period 3
lesson.summary: How the Seven Years' War, British imperial reform, colonial self-government, and Enlightenment ideas set the stage for independence and the first experiments in republican government, 1754–1800.
learningGoals: Describe the situation of the British colonies in 1754: growth, self-government, and rivalry with France.
Explain how British attempts to tighten control collided with colonists' resolve to govern themselves.
Explain how the new nation's experiments in government and its conflicts over land and trade grew out of the Revolution.
lesson.bigIdea: Period 3 begins with a war among empires and ends with a new republic, and each stage grew out of the conflict between imperial control and colonial self-government.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain the context in which America gained independence and developed a sense of national identity. For any Period 3 event, ask what came before it, what else was happening at the same time, and how both shaped it.

sections.title: The colonies in 1754

blocks.text: By 1754 the British colonies were growing quickly. They were tied to Britain by trade, print, and English political habits, and they governed themselves through elected assemblies. At the same time, the growing colonial population was expanding into the interior of North America, where it ran into French colonies and American Indian nations that depended on the fur trade and wanted to keep their lands.

The competition among the British, French, and American Indians for economic and political advantage culminated in the Seven Years' War (the French and Indian War), in which Britain defeated France and its Native allies. That victory is the starting point for nearly everything else in Period 3.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Context is the broader situation around an event, not the event itself. For the Revolution, the Seven Years' War and Britain's debts are context, while the Boston Tea Party is part of the story being explained.

sections.takeaway: A growing, self-governing set of colonies found itself in a contest with France and Native nations for the interior.

sections.title: Imperial control and self-government

blocks.text: British attempts to assert tighter control over its North American colonies and the colonial resolve to pursue self-government led to a colonial independence movement and the Revolutionary War. After 1763 Britain tried to raise revenue and manage its larger empire. Colonists who were used to governing themselves, and who drew on their rights as British subjects and on the ideas of the Enlightenment, resisted.

Protest moved from petitions and boycotts to armed conflict in 1775 and to a declaration of independence in 1776. The war that followed ended with British recognition of American independence in 1783.

sections.takeaway: Tighter British control met colonial determination to govern themselves, and the clash led to independence.

sections.title: Building a republic

blocks.text: The American Revolution's democratic and republican ideals inspired new experiments with different forms of government. The states wrote new constitutions, the Articles of Confederation created a weak national government, and the Constitution of 1787 replaced it with a stronger one. In the 1790s disagreements among leaders produced the first political parties.

The new nation also faced conflict over land, borders, and trade. Migration within North America and competition over resources intensified conflicts among peoples and nations, and the continued presence of British and Spanish power challenged the United States to protect its borders and trade. Questions about slavery and the rights of women showed that the ideals of the Revolution were not applied to everyone.

sections.takeaway: Revolutionary ideals led to new governments, new parties, and new conflicts over land, trade, and who counted as a citizen.

connections.title: A war that changed the colonies
connections.body: Topic 3.2 follows the Seven Years' War, which removed France from eastern North America and left Britain with debts and new responsibilities.
connections.transferQuestion: Which developments before 1754 help explain why colonists expected to govern themselves?
connections.feedback: A strong answer names elected assemblies, town meetings, or English legal traditions and explains how they shaped colonial expectations.
